immediate_actions: Identify and temporarily disable the affected endpoint if actively exploited
Review all database query code for string concatenation with user input
Enable detailed SQL logging to identify attempted injection payloads
fix_steps: Replace all raw SQL queries with parameterized queries or prepared statements
Use an ORM (SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, Hibernate) instead of raw SQL
Apply input validation and type checking on all user-supplied parameters
Grant database users minimum required privileges (principle of least privilege)
Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) as an additional defense layer
Run automated SQL injection tests using sqlmap in your CI/CD pipeline

code_examples.python_bad: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + user_id)

immediate_actions: Identify all output points that reflect user input without encoding
Add Content-Security-Policy header as an immediate mitigation
Review recent logs for active exploitation attempts
fix_steps: HTML-encode all user-controlled data before rendering in HTML context
Use a modern template engine with auto-escaping (Jinja2, React JSX)
Implement a strict Content-Security-Policy header
Use HttpOnly and Secure flags on all session cookies
Validate input on the server side — not just the client side
Use DOMPurify for any scenarios where HTML rendering is unavoidable

immediate_actions: Immediately block public access to the identified file via web server configuration
Rotate any credentials or secrets that may have been exposed
Check access logs to determine if the file was accessed before discovery
fix_steps: Configure web server to deny access to sensitive paths (nginx deny, Apache Deny from all)
Move configuration files outside the web root directory
Add sensitive paths to .gitignore and never commit secrets to version control
Use environment variables instead of config files for secrets
Implement periodic automated scans for exposed sensitive files
Configure a 404 response (not 403) to avoid confirming path existence

immediate_actions: Add security headers to your web server or application configuration immediately
Test headers using securityheaders.com after implementation
fix_steps: Add HSTS: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
Add CSP: Start with Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'
Add X-Frame-Options: DENY
Add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Add Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Remove Server and X-Powered-By headers
Use securityheaders.com to validate your implementation

immediate_actions: Identify which TLS versions and cipher suites are currently supported
Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 at the server configuration level
fix_steps: Enable only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 in your web server configuration
Disable weak cipher suites (RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5-based ciphers)
Use strong cipher suites: ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
Enable HSTS to force HTTPS on all connections
Use certificates from trusted CAs (Let's Encrypt is free and trusted)
Validate configuration using SSL Labs (ssllabs.com/ssltest) — aim for A+ grade
Enable OCSP stapling for improved certificate validation performance

immediate_actions: Block the dangerous port at the firewall immediately
Review access logs for unauthorized connection attempts
Check if the service has default credentials
fix_steps: Apply firewall rules to restrict port access to known IP ranges only
Move administrative services (RDP, SSH) behind a VPN
Disable Telnet and FTP — replace with SSH and SFTP respectively
Bind database services to localhost only (listen_addresses = localhost)
Enable fail2ban or equivalent brute-force protection on SSH
Disable root SSH login and enforce key-based authentication only
Regularly audit open ports: nmap -sV your-server.com

immediate_actions: Begin with DMARC in monitoring mode (p=none) to assess current email flows
fix_steps: Create SPF record: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all (adjust for your email provider)
Set up DKIM signing with your email provider and add the public key DNS record
Add DMARC record: _dmarc.example.com TXT 'v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com'
Gradually move DMARC policy from none -> quarantine -> reject
Monitor DMARC reports for legitimate sources that need SPF/DKIM alignment
Use dmarcian.com or Google Postmaster Tools to analyze reports

immediate_actions: Identify the exact CVE and assess exploitability against your configuration
Check if a patch or workaround is available from the vendor
Apply virtual patching via WAF if an official patch is not yet available
fix_steps: Update the affected software to the latest patched version immediately
Subscribe to vendor security advisories for proactive notification
Implement automated dependency scanning in your CI/CD pipeline (Dependabot, Snyk)
Create a patch management SLA: Critical CVEs patched within 24h, High within 7 days
If immediate update is not possible, apply compensating controls (firewall rules, WAF)

immediate_actions: Restrict DNS zone transfers to authorized secondary servers only
fix_steps: In BIND: add allow-transfer { <secondary-server-IP>; }; to zone configuration
In Windows DNS Server: set zone transfer permissions to named servers only
Verify fix: dig axfr @your-dns-server example.com (should fail or return REFUSED)
Audit all publicly resolvable DNS records for sensitive hostname disclosure
